# Correlation {#sec-bem-correlation}

Bali, Engle, and Murray (2016), Chapter 3, compare the cross-sectional
associations among beta, size, book-to-market (BM), and next-year excess
return. We use the 1988–2012 annual panel from
[Chapter 2](summary-statistics.qmd).

{{< include _show-table.qmd >}}
{{< include _bem-annual-betas.qmd >}}
{{< include _bem2-characteristics.qmd >}}

## Implementation

### Periodic Cross-Sectional Correlations {#annual-cross-sectional-correlations}

For variables $X$ and $Y$ in year $t$, keep the $n_t$ stocks for which
both variables are observed. The Pearson correlation measures linear
association. With $\bar X_t$ and $\bar Y_t$ denoting the means in this
paired cross-section, the correlation is

$$
\rho_t(X,Y)=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}(X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)(Y_{i,t}-\bar Y_t)}
{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}(X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)^2}
 \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}(Y_{i,t}-\bar Y_t)^2}}.
$$ {#eq-bem3-pearson}

For the Pearson entries in @tbl-bem3-annual, winsorize each variable
at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles of the paired cross-section before
computing its mean and correlation.

The Spearman correlation measures association between ranks. Let $x_{i,t}$
and $y_{i,t}$ be the ranks of the original values within the paired
cross-section, with rank 1 assigned to the smallest value. When neither
variable has ties, the rank difference $d_{i,t}=x_{i,t}-y_{i,t}$ gives

$$
\rho_t^S(X,Y)=1-\frac{6\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}d_{i,t}^2}{n_t(n_t^2-1)}.
$$ {#eq-bem3-spearman}

With ties, give equal values their average rank and compute the Pearson
correlation of the two rank vectors. This is the calculation used by
`pl.corr(method="spearman")`, including when @eq-bem3-spearman applies.

```{python}
from _bem_monthly import correlation_matrix, period_correlations

variables = {"Beta": "Beta", "Size": "Size", "BM": "BM", "excess": "Next-year return"}
annual = period_correlations(annual_panel, variables, "year").sort("year")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem3-annual
#| tbl-cap: Annual Pearson and Spearman correlations (BEM Table 3.1)
#| echo: false
return_labels = {c: c.replace("excess", "Return") for c in annual.columns if "excess" in c}
show_table(annual.rename(return_labels).rename({"year": "Year"}))
```

### Average Cross-Sectional Correlations {#average-across-years}

Average the annual coefficients for each pair. If $\mathcal T_{XY}$ is
the set of years with an available coefficient and $N_{XY}$ is its size,
the Pearson and Spearman averages are

$$
\bar\rho(X,Y)=\frac{1}{N_{XY}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_{XY}}\rho_t(X,Y)
$$ {#eq-bem3-average-pearson}

and

$$
\bar\rho^S(X,Y)=\frac{1}{N_{XY}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_{XY}}\rho_t^S(X,Y).
$$ {#eq-bem3-average-spearman}

Each available year has the same weight. The next-year return is
unavailable for the 2012 formation cohort, so return correlations are
averaged over 24 years. The other pairs use all 25 years.

```{python}
average = annual.select(pl.exclude("year").mean())
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem3-average
#| tbl-cap: Average annual correlations by pair (BEM Table 3.2)
#| echo: false
show_table(average.rename(return_labels))
```

## Interpreting Correlations {#interpret-the-correlations}

The two companion figures plot the annual coefficients in
@tbl-bem3-annual. Each panel uses formation years on the horizontal
axis. In the second figure, the return paired with year $t$ comes
from year $t+1$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bem3-characteristics
#| fig-cap: Annual correlations among beta, size, and book-to-market
#| fig-alt: Three line plots compare Pearson and Spearman correlations by formation year. Beta and size move together, while their correlations with book-to-market are usually negative.

from plotnine_polars import aes

def plot_correlations(pairs):
    labels = [f"{variables[a]} and {variables[b]}" for a, b in pairs]
    correlations = pl.concat(
        annual.select("year", Pearson=f"Pearson {a}–{b}", Spearman=f"Spearman {a}–{b}")
        .unpivot(index="year", variable_name="method", value_name="correlation")
        .with_columns(pair=pl.lit(label))
        for (a, b), label in zip(pairs, labels, strict=True)
    ).with_columns(pl.col("pair").cast(pl.Enum(labels)))
    return (
        correlations
        .ggplot(aes(x="year", y="correlation", color="method", linetype="method"))
        .geom_hline(yintercept=0, color="#b3b3b3", size=0.4)
        .geom_line(na_rm=True)
        .facet_wrap("pair", ncol=1)
        .scale_x_continuous(breaks=range(1988, 2013, 4))
        .scale_color_manual(values={"Pearson": "#24639a", "Spearman": "#ac4c27"})
        .scale_linetype_manual(values={"Pearson": "solid", "Spearman": "dashed"})
        .labs(x="Formation year", y="Correlation", color="", linetype="")
        .theme_minimal()
        .add_theme(figure_size=(8, 6), legend_position="top")
    )

plot_correlations([("Beta", "Size"), ("Beta", "BM"), ("Size", "BM")])
```

Larger stocks tend to have higher betas. Both measures of correlation
also show that larger stocks tend to have lower book-to-market ratios.
Market capitalization enters the denominator of BM, which helps explain
part of the association.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bem3-returns
#| fig-cap: Annual correlations of stock characteristics with next-year excess returns
#| fig-alt: Three line plots show Pearson and Spearman return correlations varying over formation years. The beta and return correlations turn sharply negative in 2001. The series end in 2011.
plot_correlations([("Beta", "excess"), ("Size", "excess"), ("BM", "excess")])
```

The correlations with next-year returns vary considerably. For example,
the Pearson correlation between beta and the following year's return
moves from 0.15 for the 1998 formation cohort to −0.11 for the 1999
cohort. Its average of −0.04 in @tbl-bem3-average conceals that change.

## Presenting Correlations {#present-the-correlations}

@tbl-bem3-matrix puts the same averages in a compact matrix. Read
Pearson correlations below the diagonal and Spearman correlations above
it. The Pearson correlation between size and BM is −0.22 here and
−0.23 in BEM. The other average correlations agree at the reported
precision.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem3-matrix
#| tbl-cap: Average Pearson (below diagonal) and Spearman (above diagonal) correlations (BEM Table 3.3)
#| echo: false
show_table(correlation_matrix(average.row(0, named=True), variables))
```
